title: Pyoderma gangrenosum
summary: A rare, very painful, rapidly enlarging neutrophilic ulcer with a purple undermined edge. It is not an infection. Avoid debridement and refer urgently to dermatology.

glance.think: A pustule or small wound that rapidly becomes an exquisitely painful ulcer with a violaceous, overhanging edge, often in a patient with IBD or rheumatoid arthritis.
glance.engine: Neutrophilic autoinflammation, not infection. Trauma makes it worse (pathergy).
glance.backbone: Recognise it and refer urgently. Specialist treatment with oral steroids or ciclosporin. No wide debridement.
glance.never_miss: Misdiagnosis as an infected ulcer, with repeated antibiotics and surgical debridement that make it worse.

what: Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) is a rare **neutrophilic**, autoinflammatory ulcerating skin disease. Despite the name, it is **not an infection**. It causes a rapidly enlarging, very painful ulcer with a **violaceous, undermined** border, and shows **pathergy**: it worsens after trauma or surgery.
cause: Neutrophil dysfunction and autoinflammation. About **half are idiopathic**. Associations include:

list: Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis more than Crohn’s)
Rheumatoid arthritis
Haematological malignancy and monoclonal gammopathy
Behçet disease and PAPA syndrome
Drugs, e.g. cocaine contaminated with levamisole
Starts as a pustule, papule or haemorrhagic blister, often after a **minor injury**, then becomes a deep ulcer within days.
Classic **purple, overhanging (undermined) edge** with a necrotic or purulent base.
**Severe pain**, out of proportion to the size.
Legs most often; also around stomas in IBD, and at surgical sites (pathergy).
Heals with **cribriform** (sieve-like) scars.
Clinical, after **excluding** infection, vasculitis and malignancy. Biopsy of the edge supports the diagnosis (neutrophilic infiltrate; Delphi/Maverakis criteria).
Swabs only to look for secondary infection.
**Seek dermatology urgently.**

differentials: Misdiagnosis is common. Consider venous or arterial ulcers, vasculitis, antiphospholipid syndrome ulcers, infection (ecthyma, atypical mycobacteria, deep fungal), factitious ulcers and ulcerated tumours.

management.title: Recognise and refer: do not debride
management.text: **Do not** debride or excise active PG, because pathergy makes it worse. Do not assume antibiotics will cure it. Refer **urgently** to dermatology.

list: **Oral corticosteroids** first line for rapidly progressive disease. **Ciclosporin** is an alternative first-line option.
Later lines: dapsone, tetracyclines, and biologics (e.g. **infliximab**, particularly with IBD).
Potent topical or intralesional steroid, or topical tacrolimus, for small or early lesions.
Gentle, non-adherent wound care, good **analgesia**, and treatment of the associated disease (e.g. IBD).
Monitor **blood glucose and blood pressure**.

**Bone health:** the Module 5 notes flag prednisolone **above 7.5 mg daily for 6 months or more** as an osteoporosis risk needing bone assessment (DEXA). UK guidance (NOGG) advises assessing bone health in **anyone expected to take oral steroids for 3 months or more**, so follow local policy and consider bone protection early.
Counsel on steroid cards, infection risk and not stopping abruptly.

red_flags: A painful ulcer with a **purple undermined edge** that expands over days.
An ulcer getting worse after debridement or surgery (pathergy).
Systemic upset, or rapid spread despite antibiotics.
pearls: **Pathergy counselling:** protect the skin, and plan procedures only when the disease is quiet, with specialist input.
In the community, escalate early. Do not trial antibiotic after antibiotic.
Ask about bowel symptoms and joint pain. PG can be the first sign of IBD.
